rv.q: For the rest of us, a real musical comedy

A real-life musical celebrating willful delusion in the name of Broadway is perhaps the best possible tribute to the Smash of yore, and an enjoyable two-and-a-half hours at the theater for everyone else.
Either way, it is, in fact, what you've been needing.

But as they extend into the second act, the busy convolutions of the plot—will Ivy, Karen or Chloe ultimately win the role of Marilyn, and does one really care?—become repetitive and mildly preposterous, even for the purportedly madcap world of showbiz.
Somehow, I enjoyed the overall experience of Smash.
Smash The Musical confounds at least as often as it pleases.

Once a deliciously hate-watchable prime-time NBC drama with a killer pilot and a steep drop-off in quality, Smash has gone through more than a decade of reworking, including attempts to stage the musical-within-the-show straight-up, and has finally arrived on Broadway overmasticated and gummy.
Despite best efforts from all, the whole thing feels like a burger smashed onto a grill manned by Father Time, a charred remnant of days fast gone by.
Elice and Martin have salted the whole thing with disdain.
Now, twelve years later, much of the backstage drama’s creative team has doubled-down on their failure and produced something far, far worse.
Smash is a smashing celebration of the joy of theater.
With its transition to the stage, Smash finally realizes its full potential as a hilarious, pointed satire that both skewers and celebrates the Great White Way.

Smash has a ruthlessness that’s hard to believe exists in the PR’d universe of modern theater, and it does sometimes curdle. There’s an ickiness to Ivy’s story, where a woman attempting to self-actualize and improve herself is treated as an impediment.
She's one of the few legitimate triple threats that we have on Broadway right now
This is sheer entertainment with thrilling performances and back-to-back laughs.

We all love a peek behind the curtain, indulging in some schadenfreude as we experience the agony and the ecstasy, as it were, from the comfort of our theater seat. SMASH mostly delivers on this promise with broad comedy, flashy, old school musical numbers and delicious backstage drama.
The show is fun but not cutting edge or unforgettable.
The “Smash” ensemble, led by Hurder and Nielsen, make it better than first-rate.
Despite having an all-around talented cast and a strong foundation of song-and-dance material , Smash doesn't quite live up to its title.
They promised us The Producers, and they gave us Parade.
It’s overstuffed with silliness like that, and Susan Stroman, who usually has some clever tricks up her sleeve, isn’t able to rein this one in.
200 bucks for a ticket. I can stay home and be depressed for free.
Bombshell suffers from an identity crisis. So does Smash.

Although Smash is not so hot as light entertainment, its script and score are at least professionally executed and the leading actors, capably supported by an attractive ensemble, all but knock themselves out striving to put over this dubious endeavor.
The result is more of a splat than a smash.
The laborious dud of a musical now bearing its name doesn’t seem to know what it is, and its most needless act of self-sabotage is that it screws its own fans over.
It’s “Smash” through a funhouse mirror: recognizable in outline, but warped in execution—less a love letter to Broadway than a Post
Indeed, this misbegotten, meshugana mess wastes the talent of a top-notch cast and an often-delightful score from Marc Shaiman and Scott Wittman, not to mention 2 ½ hours of your time.
To put it simply, Smash is stunning; it surprised me with it’s depth and also delivered a beautiful performance.
Smash lives up to its name with an over-the-top theatricality and cheekiness that pulls back the curtain on the business of Broadway with a wink and a nod.
So much talent and so much promising raw material is squandered in the service of a story whose dark humor turns caustic and distasteful.
As for me, I'm afraid I'll be looking elsewhere.

cn.t: Critics are divided on this meta-musical adaptation of the NBC series, with some finding it a gleefully bonkers guilty pleasure while others dismiss it as a messy, tasteless spectacle that wastes its talented cast and catchy score.

sg.ra: Imperial's auditorium is rectangular and wider than it is deep, so you lose very little distance moving back from the premium C-G band — and once you clear the mezzanine overhang (which hangs over Orchestra row H) the rake picks up enough to see over heads. Multiple Chess (2026) and Water for Elephants (2024) sitters in rows H-P described a dead-center full-stage view at sub-premium prices; one Chess viewer at Orch C H106 called it 'the best broadway seats I've had.' Seatplan, TickPick, and Headout independently pick this same band as the value tier.

TickPick and Seatplan both explicitly recommend Front Mezz row C and back (centered) over rows A-B, because the Imperial's front-mezz railing sits high enough to clip the stage for front-row sitters — a Water for Elephants viewer at Front Mezz R A401 (self-reported 6'3") wrote 'The bar definitely gets in the way… Avoid.' Rows C-F clear that bar while keeping the whole-stage overhead view that's the main reason to choose mezzanine over orchestra at Imperial.

sg.vl: Steep rake saves the cheap seats
sg.ra: Imperial has no elevators/escalators and the rear mezz is a real climb (one Chess sitter called it 'quite the hike'), but the rake is steep enough that several Chess and Smash viewers reported unobstructed full-stage views from rows A-C even with tall people in front ('Rake is good so most likely no heads blocking the stage,' 'Theater has a good rake so you can see over the person in front of you'). TickPick and Headout both specifically recommend rear-mezz center (not sides) as the cheap-seat sweet spot here.

sg.vl: Under the overhang, far from the action
sg.ra: Imperial is wider than it is deep, so the penalty for sitting far back is real — you lose closeness without gaining much sightline, and the same mid-tier price bracket gets you a few rows forward.
